title: OpenAI and Georgia county leaders hit with Mafia-style RICO racketeering lawsuit
content:
OpenAI and Georgia county leaders hit with Mafia-style RICO racketeering lawsuit over $30 billion AI data center — residents allege closed-door conspiracy and NDAs were used to push 3.2-gigawatt ‘Project Camellia’ through
Data center mafia.
Residents of Effingham County, Georgia, just filed a RICO lawsuit against their county commissioners, county leaders, and OpenAI and its affiliates, alleging that they committed various offenses in a conspiracy to get OpenAI’s “Project Camellia” approved. According to the Effingham Herald, the plaintiffs — Dr. Michelle Finch-Mincey, Lehman Mincey Jr., and Raymond Carver — are seeking civil damages, saying that the project has harmed their property values and even pointing out that purchase offers for nearby residential properties have dropped or been withdrawn since the data center was announced.
The lawsuit names all Effingham County Commissioners — Chairperson Damon Rahn, Forrest Floyd, Roger Burdette, Jamie DeLoach, Elizabeth Helmly, and Phil Kieffer — as defendants, alongside County Manager Tim Callanan, Effingham County Industrial Development Authority (IDA) CEO Brandt Herndon, the IDA itself, OpenAI, Octans GA LLC, the entity operating the data center on behalf of OpenAI, and Savannah Industrial Development LLC, the agency involved in the sale of IDA property to Octans and OpenAI.
It’s alleged that the defendants committed fraud and concealment through non-disclosure agreements and misleading public statements so that residents remain unaware of the nature of the projects for as long as possible, and that there was a civil conspiracy “to advance Project Camellia through confidential negotiations and closed-door decisions.” They also claimed that the parties engaged in improper land transactions, zoning violations, and civil racketeering.w
Project Camellia is one of OpenAI’s biggest data center projects planned for construction in Effingham County. The site is expected to cost somewhere between $20 billion and $30 billion, to be built across five phases, with a planned compute capacity of 3.2 gigawatts. The company also promised that it will not affect the community’s utility costs, as it will pay for the full cost of all its required infrastructure upgrades, and that it will have minimal water use due to its closed-loop water system. Despite those promises, it seems that some people are opposing the project because of how the county had allegedly tried to secure the land, tax incentives, and zoning approvals without informing the residents until key decisions were finalized and contracts had been signed.
The RICO Act — or Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act — was originally conceived as a way to counter organized crime, particularly Mafia leadership, who often used low-level members to commit individual crimes and do the dirty work for them. However, Georgia’s RICO Act is less stringent than the federal version, which is why it’s been used multiple times for cases that seemingly had nothing to do with the Mafia. For example, it was in the 2023 election racketeering case against Donald Trump and 18 others in the attempt to overturn the 2020 U.S. presidential election results in the state, and it was also used in Young Thug’s trial after the rapper was accused of running YSL Records as a criminal street gang.
Critics say that Georgia’s version is way too encompassing, though, and that it was being used to squeeze defendants involved in more mundane or common felonies. “When you have a hammer, everything looks like a nail,” Georgia State University professor of criminal justice and criminology Volkan Topalli said in Atlanta Magazine.
The actions of both state officials, OpenAI, and its affiliates are not new, though. There have already been multiple complaints of data center developers and local governments using non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) while they negotiate terms for possible data center projects. Developers say they use this tool to avoid “running afoul of insider trading rules,” but people have pointed out that West Feliciana Parish in Louisiana was able to close a data center deal without resorting to one. An AWS data center in Gilroy, California, is also facing scrutiny after residents only discovered the nature of the project when construction began after a five-year permitting saga that relied on zoning rules that were set 45 years ago.

report.summary: Residents of Effingham County, Georgia, filed a RICO lawsuit alleging county officials and OpenAI affiliates conspired through NDAs and closed-door deals to approve a 3.2-GW data center.
report.background: AI's power-hungry data center boom is colliding with local land-use politics. OpenAI's Project Camellia in Effingham County is planned as a $20 billion-$30 billion, five-phase campus with 3.2 gigawatts of compute capacity. OpenAI says it will pay for infrastructure upgrades and use a closed-loop water system to minimize impacts. But residents allege they were kept in the dark while commissioners, the county industrial authority, OpenAI and affiliated LLCs negotiated land, tax incentives and zoning through NDAs and nonpublic meetings. The case leans on Georgia's RICO statute, which is broader than the federal anti-Mafia law and has been used in high-profile cases including the 2023 Trump election racketeering case and the Young Thug trial. Similar disputes have erupted over data center secrecy in Louisiana and California.
key_points: The lawsuit names all Effingham County commissioners, the county manager, the industrial development authority and its CEO, OpenAI, Octans GA LLC and Savannah Industrial Development LLC. Plaintiffs allege fraud, concealment through NDAs, misleading public statements, improper land transactions, zoning violations and civil racketeering in a coordinated scheme to approve Project Camellia.

Project Camellia is one of OpenAI's largest planned data centers: a $20 billion-$30 billion campus built in five phases with 3.2 gigawatts of compute capacity. OpenAI promised the project would not raise community utility costs because it would pay for infrastructure upgrades, and that a closed-loop water system would keep water use minimal.

The case uses Georgia's RICO law, originally designed to fight organized crime but broader than the federal version. It has been used in the Trump election case and Young Thug's trial. Critics say Georgia's statute is overbroad, quoting a criminologist: 'When you have a hammer, everything looks like a nail.'

The plaintiffs say nearby home purchase offers have dropped or been withdrawn since the data center was announced, harming property values. They argue residents were not told the full nature of the project until key decisions were finalized, despite public promises about utility and water impacts.

The lawsuit highlights a wider pattern: data center developers and local governments often use NDAs during negotiations. Developers say secrecy avoids insider-trading problems, but critics note some communities have closed data center deals without NDAs, and an AWS project in Gilroy, California, drew scrutiny after residents learned details only when construction began.
report.impact: The lawsuit raises legal and reputational risk for AI companies racing to secure power and land. If it advances, it could force more transparency in data center siting, making NDAs, tax incentives and closed-door negotiations subject to litigation and public-records scrutiny. For developers, the case is a warning that community opposition can escalate beyond zoning hearings into racketeering claims, potentially delaying projects and raising costs. For regular users, the dispute may slow some AI infrastructure buildouts, but it also tests whether local residents can challenge secrecy around projects that affect property values, utilities and land use. The outcome could shape how AI firms engage with host communities nationwide.
report.tools: To follow similar projects, use MuckRock to file public-records requests for county meeting minutes, NDAs and incentive agreements; OpenCorporates to trace LLCs and corporate affiliates; OpenStreetMap and Data Center Map to track planned facilities; and local planning-commission portals for zoning and permit documents. These tools help residents and journalists compare public promises with actual contracts and land-use decisions.
